p01-ancestry-vs-class.ambiguity: §5.1 'class precedence is absolute ... even when the witness is a descendant' vs §5.2 'descendant wins' within a class. Does an override that is an ANCESTOR beat a task that is its DESCENDANT?

p02-witness-descendant-of-task.ambiguity: Same question, the other direction: a witness that DESCENDS from the task. The spec's parenthetical suggests task wins; a naive reading of 'descendant wins' gives the witness.

p07-orphan-descendant.ambiguity: §5.5 'the orphan's descendants are NOT auto-orphaned'. Does the descendant's OWN effects then apply, or is it excluded because its ancestor is missing?
p07-orphan-descendant.declared_split: kid-applies -> y present ; whole-branch-excluded -> y absent

p10-id-whitespace-and-separators.ambiguity: §1 says ids must be free of \n and :. Is that enforced (reject) or merely documented? The corpus cannot tell, but a port that rejects and a port that accepts will diverge on a hostile input.

p12-kind-null.ambiguity: 1.1 says kind defaults to null and other values are 'out of scope for the fold'; 5.1 ranks every record by class. What class does a null-kind record have?
p12-kind-null.declared_split: null ranks last -> x=from-override ; null throws ; null inherits witness -> x=from-null

p13-class-vs-ancestry-inversion.ambiguity: 5.1's parenthetical mentions ancestry as an exception. Does that generalise to 'class beats ancestry' everywhere, or is ancestry only a tie-break within a class?
p13-class-vs-ancestry-inversion.declared_split: class-absolute -> x=1 (witness loses despite descending) ; ancestry-first -> x=2
